The Streaked shearwater (Calonectris leucomelas) is a pelagic procellariiform that breeds colonially on islands off eastern Asia. Like its congener Calonectris diomedea, this species exhibits prolonged incubation periods; eggs maintained under natural nest conditions at approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically hatch after 55 days [ab = 55 days], a developmental duration that reflects the substantial energy reserves allocated to the slowly developing embryo. Newly hatched chicks, still wet from the egg, weigh approximately 59 grams [Wwb = approximately 59 grams], a relatively modest mass that underscores the altricial-to-semi-precocial spectrum observed in shearwaters. This initial wet weight at birth is followed by a rapid phase of mass gain, as the nestling is brooded and provisioned by both parents. The thermal regime of the nest burrow, which buffers against surface temperature fluctuations, remains crucial during this early period, with internal chamber temperatures often stabilizing near 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during the incubation phase. Direct parental contact and the insulating properties of the burrow help maintain the required thermal environment for successful embryonic and early post-hatching development.

As the chick progresses through the nestling stage, it embarks on a trajectory of accelerated somatic growth that culminates in the achievement of an ultimate wet weight asymptote. Field measurements on Mikura Island indicate that the asymptotic mass for nestlings of Calonectris leucomelas reaches approximately 720 grams [Wwi = approximately 720 grams], a value that approaches the typical adult body mass for the species. This ultimate wet weight is attained after several weeks of intensive parental provisioning, during which the growing chick is fed a lipid-rich diet of fish and squid. The growth rate during this period is remarkable; the chick must more than decuple its hatchling mass in preparation for the energetic demands of flight and dispersal. This rapid biomass accumulation is supported by the efficient conversion of ingested prey into body tissue, a strategy common among procellariiforms that accumulate substantial fat reserves prior to fledging. The nestling remains dependent on its parents throughout this entire period, gradually developing its flight feathers and thermoregulatory capacity before it is ready to depart the burrow.

The developmental timeline of the Streaked shearwater culminates in fledging, a critical life-history transition that occurs under the physiological conditions typical of an active, endothermic juvenile. At the core body temperature characteristic of flight-capable individuals, approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the time since birth at fledging has been documented at 97 days [tx = 97 days]. This pre-fledging interval encompasses the entire period from hatching to the first sustained flight, during which the nestling completes feather development, strengthens its flight muscles, and depletes the remaining yolk-derived nutrients. The timing of this event is tightly linked to local oceanographic productivity, as successful fledging depends on the bird having accrued sufficient energy reserves to sustain it during the post-fledging dispersal phase. Once the chick leaves the burrow, it becomes independent of its parents and must immediately forage for itself. This transition represents a major physiological and behavioral shift, marking the onset of the juvenile stage in the species' life cycle.

Sexual maturation in the Streaked shearwater is a protracted process, as is typical for long-lived seabirds with delayed reproduction. Puberty, defined as the attainment of gonadal maturity, occurs at 291 days since birth [tp = 291 days since birth] when birds are maintained at an ambient temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], a thermal condition that approximates the core body temperature of active adults. This relatively brief interval to puberty, however, does not correspond to immediate breeding. In most procellariiforms, including this species, there is a significant lag between the achievement of physiological maturity and the onset of actual reproductive activity. First-year and even second-year birds frequently return to the colony but do not engage in nesting, instead spending time prospecting for future mates and suitable burrow sites. This delay is thought to reflect the need for young birds to perfect their foraging skills and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the high energetic costs of egg production and chick rearing. The 291-day figure (291 days since birth) [tp = 291 days since birth] therefore represents the earliest point at which the reproductive system is functional, not the age at which a bird first contributes to the next generation at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].

The reproductive schedule of the Streaked shearwater is characterized by extreme iteroparity, a strategy that buffers the population against periodic reproductive failures caused by storms or food shortages. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed in terms of annual output, translates to one egg per year [Ri = one egg per year]. Under the thermal conditions of an active adult (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), the time since birth at first brood is approximately 3 years [tR = approximately 3 years], a value that aligns closely with records for the closely related Calonectris diomedea. This delayed onset of first reproduction is compensated by an exceptionally long lifespan; the maximum recorded longevity for Calonectris leucomelas is estimated at 24.8 years [am = 24.8 years] when measured at a core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. Such a prolonged adult life stage allows individuals to accumulate multiple breeding attempts over decades, with each single-egg clutch representing a relatively modest but sustained investment that extends across many seasons.
